usage: There is a thing / I have something
There are a lot of things
examples: There are a lot of things in the bag.
nuance: 물건 is the all-purpose word for a physical object or item, used when you do not know or do not need to name the exact thing. In shops it also means merchandise or goods. It is concrete: you cannot use 물건 for abstract things like ideas or feelings.
mistakes: Do not use 물건 for abstract 'things' like plans or feelings — use 일 or 것 instead.
물건 is a noun, not a counter; to count items use 개 (한 개, 두 개), not '한 물건'.

nuance: 상자 is a box or carton, usually made of cardboard or hard material, used for holding or shipping things. The Sino-Korean 박스 (from English 'box') is also common in daily speech, but 상자 is the standard native-feeling word. Count boxes with 개: 상자 한 개.
mistakes: Do not confuse 상자 (box) with 봉투 (envelope) or 봉지 (bag) — those are soft containers.
For a very small jewelry-type case Koreans often say 케이스 or 갑, not 상자.

examples: Please give me one sheet of paper.
Please write your name on this paper.
There's no paper. What should I do?
nuance: 종이 is paper as a material or a sheet. To count sheets use the counter 장 (한 장, 두 장), the same counter used for tickets and photos. Note that 신문 (newspaper) and 책 (book) are separate words even though they are made of 종이.
mistakes: Count paper with 장, not 개 — say 종이 한 장, not 종이 한 개.
Do not say 종이 for a document you fill out; that is 서류 or just the form name.

usage: Please give me a plastic bag
I put it in a plastic bag
Do you have a plastic bag?
examples: Please give me one plastic bag.
I put the fruit in a plastic bag.
Bags are often paid for in Korea
nuance: 비닐봉지 is a thin plastic (vinyl) bag, the kind you get at shops and markets. Koreans often shorten it to just 봉지 or even 비닐 in casual speech. Since plastic bags usually cost money in Korean stores, asking 비닐봉지 주세요 is a very common everyday phrase.
mistakes: 비닐 here means 'plastic/vinyl', not the English 'vinyl' records — do not mix the meanings.
A paper or cloth shopping bag is 가방 or 봉투, not 비닐봉지.

usage: I put it in the basket
examples: Please put the fruit in the basket.
I picked up a basket at the mart.
nuance: 바구니 is a basket — an open container with handles for carrying or holding things, like a shopping basket or laundry basket. It is often combined with another noun: 빨래 바구니 (laundry basket), 장바구니 (shopping/grocery basket). For an online shopping cart, Koreans use 장바구니.
mistakes: A shopping cart with wheels is 카트, while a hand-held basket is 바구니.
Do not confuse 바구니 (open basket) with 상자 (closed box).

usage: I fill the bucket with water
examples: Please fill the bucket with water.
I use a bucket when I clean.
nuance: 양동이 is a bucket or pail, typically used to hold water for cleaning. In everyday speech many Koreans just say 바께쓰 (a loanword) or 통, but 양동이 is the standard word and the safe one to learn. Use 담다 or 받다 with water going into it.
mistakes: Do not confuse 양동이 (bucket) with 그릇 (bowl/dish) — a bucket is bigger and for carrying water.
양동이 is one word; do not split it into 양 동이.

examples: I threw away the empty can.
There is candy inside the can.
nuance: 깡통 is a metal can or tin, like a drink can or a food tin. The verb for opening a can is 따다 (the same verb used for opening a bottle). Empty cans go in the 캔 recycling, and Koreans also use the loanword 캔 especially for drink cans (음료수 캔).
mistakes: Open a can with 따다, not 열다 (열다 is for doors and lids).
For a drink can specifically, 캔 is very common; 깡통 can sound a bit more general or old-fashioned.

usage: I lock it (put the lock on)
examples: I put a lock on the door.
Where is the key for the lock?
nuance: 자물쇠 is a physical lock or padlock — the device itself, opened with a 열쇠 (key). For a digital door lock Koreans say 도어록 or 번호키. Use 채우다/잠그다 to lock and 풀다/열다 to unlock; 잠그다 is the verb for locking in general.
mistakes: Do not confuse 자물쇠 (lock) with 열쇠 (key) — they are opposite halves of the pair.
An apartment keypad lock is 도어록 or 번호키, not 자물쇠.

examples: Please hold the handle on the bus.
nuance: 손잡이 literally combines 손 (hand) + 잡이 (the holding part), meaning the handle, knob, or grip you grab — on a door, bag, cup, or the strap/handle on a bus. It is very productive in compounds: 문 손잡이 (door handle), 컵 손잡이 (cup handle). Use 잡다 (hold) or 돌리다 (turn) with it.
mistakes: 손잡이 covers many kinds of handles; do not search for a separate word for each object.
Hold a handle with 잡다, not 들다 (which means to lift the whole object).

examples: The bag's strap is too long.
I tied the box with string.
nuance: 끈 is a flexible string, cord, or strap used for tying or carrying — shoelaces (신발 끈), bag straps (가방 끈), apron ties. It is thicker than 실 (thread) and is what you use to bind or fasten. Pair it with 묶다 (tie) and 풀다 (untie).
mistakes: Do not confuse 끈 (string/strap) with 실 (thin sewing thread) or 줄 (line/rope, also 'queue').
끈 is one syllable; remember the ㄲ double consonant and the ㄴ batchim.

examples: I sewed on a button with a needle.
nuance: 바늘 is a needle — a thin, sharp tool for sewing, used together with 실 (thread). The same word also means the hands of a clock (시계 바늘) and a syringe needle (주삿바늘). It is sharp, so it pairs naturally with 뾰족하다 (pointy).
mistakes: Do not confuse 바늘 (needle) with 바늘구멍 (the eye/hole of a needle).
You thread 실 (thread) through a 바늘 — the verb is 꿰다, not 묶다.

examples: Do you have a needle and thread?
I sewed the button on with red thread.
단추를 달다 = sew on a button
nuance: 실 is thread or yarn — the thin strand used for sewing or knitting, paired with 바늘 (needle). It is much finer than 끈 (string/cord). The natural counter for a single strand is 가닥 (한 가닥), and 실 is part of compounds like 실타래 (a skein of thread).
mistakes: Do not confuse 실 (sewing thread) with 끈 (thicker string/strap).
실 is also a prefix meaning 'real/actual' in other words (실시간); here it is the standalone noun 'thread'.

examples: A button came off my shirt.
nuance: 단추 is a clothing button — the kind you fasten and unfasten on a shirt or coat. Use 채우다 (or 잠그다) to button up and 풀다 to unbutton; 달다 to sew one on. Note this is the clothing button; a button you press on a machine is 버튼.
mistakes: A press button on a device or remote is 버튼, not 단추 — 단추 is for clothing.
Button up with 채우다/잠그다, not 묶다.

examples: It's raining. Do you have an umbrella?
I left my umbrella on the subway.
nuance: 우산 is an umbrella for rain. The verb to put one up or use it is 쓰다 (the same verb as wearing a hat or glasses). A folding umbrella is 접는 우산 or 3단 우산, and a parasol for sun is 양산 — a different word.
mistakes: Put up / use an umbrella with 쓰다, not 입다 (which is for clothes you wear on the body).
A sun parasol is 양산, not 우산 — 우산 is specifically for rain.
